input: A shell-and-tube exchanger forming part of the refinery preheat train is used to heat crude oil, and in the run reported here it operates with a duty of 1088 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, while the crude enters at 30 °C and leaves at 55 °C. Working from the stream temperatures, the terminal differences come out at 95 K at the hot end and 80 K at the cold end, and the log-mean temperature difference calculated from those two values is 87.3 K. With the installed area of 56.7 m2, the duty and the log-mean difference together give an overall coefficient of 220 W m-2 K-1. It should be understood that this coefficient is the operating value for the run as a whole. It bundles together the two film resistances, the wall, and whatever fouling had accumulated over the course of the run, and no part of it can be separated out by these measurements. The smaller terminal difference stands at the cold end, so the cold end is where a change in either stream temperature moves the driving force most, and where the exchanger reaches its closest approach. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, so the fouling share of the coefficient cannot be split from the clean value on the basis of this evidence. A second run after cleaning would give that split; on one run the two are necessarily reported together. Overall, the exchanger met the stated duty at the stated temperatures over the run. How the coefficient moves as fouling builds, and what it returns to after cleaning, are both open questions on the basis of a single run, and the reported coefficient should be read as a run-average value at the tested conditions.
